questions.question: When will quantum computers actually be useful?

hybrid.answer:
Quantum computers start to be useful with the first clear quantum advantage, which I expect in 2026, and the transformational impact comes by 2030, when we expect the first fault-tolerant machine. [1][2]

**Near term (first advantage):** At IBM, our roadmap says that by 2026 we will have the first real quantum advantage, meaning an application on a real system that can't be done with classical computing alone. [2] The first applications I expect are in chemistry and catalysis, for example simulating the catalytic action of complex enzymes. [3] In finance, a partner of ours, HSBC, reported 34% better accuracy in predicting whether a stock order gets filled at a given price, though we don't have proof that a classical computer couldn't do it. [4]

**By 2030 (transformational):** By 2030 we will have the first fault-tolerant machine, one that implements universal quantum computing and brings the transformational impact. [1] That is five years of work, so it falls within this decade. [1]

**Why I trust the timeline:** A technology is real when it has a roadmap you can show was met in the past. [5] At IBM we have sustained ours year by year and never missed a point on it. [2]

**Useful already, in a limited way:** Even without full error correction, we can mitigate errors. Scaling is still exponential but slower, so we can get value today by starting to simulate small molecules. [6]

One caveat: this is IBM's roadmap and my expectation, not a guarantee.

questions.question: Should banks be worried about quantum computers breaking encryption?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. Banks should act now, because I think we are already late. [1]

**Why it matters:** At IBM, our roadmap points to the first fault-tolerant quantum computing machine by 2030. [2] When that arrives, public-key (asymmetric) cryptography will be attacked and stop working. That is the cryptography behind secure internet connections, digital signatures, secure data transmission and secure digital currency. [3]

**Why waiting is risky:** Solutions already exist for moving to something secure against quantum attacks, but you have to start now rather than wait and hope I'm wrong. [1] Someone is already collecting encrypted data in circulation and storing it. Once they have the capability, they can go back, read that data and even forge digital signatures and contracts. [4]

**What I'd do:** Move now, and do it in a way that builds in crypto agility, so you can migrate from one cryptography to another easily. [5] Nobody can guarantee that the quantum-safe algorithms we have today will stay secure forever. Cryptography by definition is not secure forever. [5]

questions.question: What about the energy cost of all this AI?

hybrid.answer:
My view is that the energy cost can be cut by an order of magnitude if we build AI the right way: many specialized models with an orchestrator on top, rather than one giant model that does everything.

**Why one giant model is a problem.** A single model that integrates all the data and modalities could bring many discoveries, but it is hugely expensive, especially in use, since training happens once while use happens a million times [1]. Using a model with 1,000 trillion parameters just to decide where to go for dinner makes no sense [1]. Training energy also doesn't scale linearly with model size; it grows at least quadratically [1].

**What I'd do instead.** Build around 100 models of roughly 1 trillion parameters each, specialized by task, modality or use case. An orchestrator on top, which can itself be an AI model (the agentic AI idea), calls the individual models and integrates their answers [2]. Because the cost grows quadratically, the sum of the smaller models' costs is much lower than that of the one big model. Done right, this gives results with an order of magnitude less energy, and also more accurate ones [2].

**Accuracy too.** These models only learn sequences and predict what comes next. If you mix too many uncorrelated things, they can give nonsensical answers, as with a recipe in the kitchen versus a recipe in chemistry [3].

**Avoiding duplicated work.** I also push for building base models once, openly and collaboratively, so people don't redo the same models with lots of compute and CO2 emissions to reach the same result [4].
